lines.speaker: Damian Penner
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Damian Penner (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. Steinbach has gained national accolades as once again Steinbach citizens rose up and donated a median average that tops all metropolitan and census agglomerations. What is most amazing about this is not that Steinbach citizens are some of the most generous individuals in our nation, but the margin by which Steinbach stands out. The national median average for donations of 20— for 2021 was $360. That's national. In Manitoba, that rose up to $550, but in Steinbach, it skyrocketed all the way up to $2,270. That is a staggering 6 times the national average and just over 4 times the provincial average, with nearly 1 in 4 individuals claiming a donation in 2021. Steinbach citizens, you need to give yourselves a pat on the back. While the black and white dollars and cents of Steinbach's generosity can easily be measured through tax filings, there is another area of excellence that I feel Steinbach could easily be top of the nation in, and that is the generosity that our citizens are willing to give in their time. If you think of all the organizations that are able to operate in Steinbach due to their dedicated volunteer base, the list quickly becomes quite long, especially considering the humble size of our city. Steinbach as a city gets part of its identity from the many festivals it hosts every year. All the activities at the Mennonite Heritage Village, Pioneer Days and the parade that's involved, the upcoming IRL Festival, and of course the weekend-long Summer in the City. These events take hundreds, if not thousands, of volunteer hours to be able to pull off. And not only do these events occur, they are done with excellence. If you were to just take the Mennonite Heritage Village and all the displays, activities, tour guides, and other volunteers that keep that museum going, it would add up into thousands of volunteer hours every year. Think of Spring on the Farm, Pioneer Days, and Fall on the Farm, and how it is a bustling area of activity. With plows going, horse rides, and of course my favorite, the team working the vintage threshing machine. To me, generosity is a trait that you see in true leaders and individuals with influence. If you've ever hung around somebody that is stingy, you see it permeate through their everyday life, and they're often miserable to be around. In the inverse, an individual with a generous heart often has joy, exudes an inner peace and selflessness to build up others around them. and the community they live in. Generosity changes your mindset from a place of, what can I do for myself, to what can we all do for each other, and our city shows that at every turn. So why are Steinbach citizens so generous with not only their wallets but also their time? One could say it's due to historically large religious community that calls individuals to a purpose of something greater than themselves. Perhaps it's a culture that has been passed down from generate— Thank you. from parents to future generations. Could even be attributed to events like Steinbach's Pick Up and Walk that intentionally involves entire families coming together and introducing children to a spirit of generosity and volunteerism as early as some of them can walk. Regardless of what the reason is, I am proud of our citizens and our community for their generous hearts and generous actions throughout the year, and I applaud you all. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Mr. Mayor and members of council, the administration of the city and particularly our senior manager of finance, Brian Hrehirchuk, have spent countless hours in preparing its annual budget documents, and I will turn it over to Mr. Hrehirchuk to present the city's budget. I'm pleased to present the city's 2023 financial plan and related information for council and for purposes of the public hearing.

lines.speaker: Brian Hrehirchuk
lines.title: Senior Manager, Finance
lines.label: Brian Hrehirchuk (Senior Manager, Finance)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor, members of council. I'm pleased to be presenting the city's 2023 Financial plan to highlight some of the main items that are planned for the year. The annual budget cycle is almost a continuous process. For the 2023 budget year, it started early in 2022. Throughout the process, input is provided by staff, management, and council. The financial plan being presented today is based on the recommendations of council provided at their final review in November. Some of the highlights for 2023 include a municipal mill rate of 13.7 mills, which is a decrease of 2.8% from 2022. Utility rates are expected to increase by an average of 4%, pending approval by the Public Utilities Board. Residential garbage collection rates will increase by 2.7%, while most fees for permits and land use applications will increase by 2.5%. The overall capital program for 2023 is budgeted at $67.3 million. Some of the larger budgeted projects include construction on the event center, the Loewen PTH 12 intersection renewal, Lift Station Number 2 upgrade, as well as the Park Road West upgrade. Overall, projected revenues for 2023 are just over $34.5 million. Similar to other years, property taxes are the city's largest source of revenue, accounting for roughly half of the overall revenue amount. For 2023, there was a property value growth of 10.8%. Commercial properties make up about 25% of the total property values in the city, and with the provincial portioning system, a lower portion of residential property values are subject to property tax than commercial property values. As I mentioned earlier, the property tax rate of 13.7 mills is down 2.8% from From 2022. Roughly half of the municipal revenues are from property taxes. $18 million is to be raised by property taxes in 2023. The city is also required to collect the education and school taxes on behalf of the province and Hanover School Division. As in previous years, this is projected to make up roughly half of the total tax revenue collected by the city. The average market value for a dwelling in Steinbach is roughly $217,000. Based on this and the budgeted municipal mill rate, the average city property tax bill works out to around $111 per month. In addition to regular property taxes, supplementary property taxes are levied on new construction or where there was an addition or improvement to increase the value of the property. This is expected to provide an additional $550,000 in 2023. Federal and provincial operating grants have also been a consistent source of revenue for the city. The provincial per capita tax sharing grant is expected to provide $3 million in 2023, while the federal gas tax grant will provide just over $890,000. One of the main non-tax revenues for the city is from user fees. These are fees paid by those who benefit from the service provided. Some services compete with the open market, but a number of rates may be subsidized for programs to be accessible. Development in Steinbach stayed strong in 2022 with just under $80 million in total permit values. This activity is expected to continue into 2023 and beyond. Now we will look at some of the programs that are funded by these revenues. Overall, the expenses are equal to the projected revenues at just over $34.5 million. Some, some 2023 programs include waste reduction and recycling at just over $1 million. Support for the Jake Epp Public Library at $454,000 and various other programs as listed. Every year, the city provides grants for various organizations throughout the city. In 2023, these grants total almost $1.3 million, the recipients as listed. One of the largest city expenses is that of our employees. The total labor cost, including benefits, for 2023 is budgeted at $10.7 million, or roughly a third of the city's operating budget. Of this total, the aquatic center makes up about 20% of the total labor hours. The largest of any city department. Protective services includes 18 RCMP officers, 49 firefighters, and a community services officer to enforce city bylaws. The total cost of these services is budgeted at $4.6 million for the upcoming year. The city currently has over 140 kilometers of road service— surface. The maintenance for this infrastructure can depend fairly significantly on the weather in any given year, and for 2023 is expected to cost $2.8 million. Solid waste services. We provide both curbside and on-demand pickup services to both residential and commercial properties. The cost of providing these services is expected to reach $3 million for the upcoming year, which is funded by user fees. Our primary recreation facilities include the aquatic centre, arena, A.D. Penner Park, curling rink, and soccer park. as well as various green space and parks around the city. The expected cost of operating and maintaining these facilities is budgeted at $4.6 million for 2023. Both the number of customers serviced by the water and wastewater utility and the length of underground infrastructure network continue to grow. The expected cost to maintain this infrastructure and provide the utility services is expected to be $4.2 million in 2023. In addition to the typical operating expenses that the city regularly incurs, larger projects also require significant funding. Some of this comes from reserve funds that have been saved in previous years, while while other projects will require debt funding. Some of the main projects for the upcoming year include equipment replacement, the event centre construction, and PTH 12 Loewen intersection. The total capital program for the year is expected to be just over $67 million. The city will periodically issue debt in order to add or renew various infrastructure or facilities throughout the city. Each loan will fund a specific project. In 2023, 5 projects have a debt component: the event center construction, lift station number 2 upgrade, the Loewen PTH 12 intersection, fire department ladder truck, and Barkman Avenue renewal. This is expected to create just over $12 million of new debt while $2.1 million of previously issued debt will be paid off. The city continues to use a 5-year amortization term for all of its debt, allowing us to borrow at lower interest rates than if a longer term was used. Our average interest rate for 2023 is just over 2.4%, while the debt balance at the end of the year is expected to be slightly over $14 million. Payments that are required for previously issued debt will total $2.2 million in 2023. Of this amount, $98,000 is interest. Funding for these debt payments is raised through property taxation, and for 2023, $1.8 mils will be required to raise the necessary funds. This equates to just over 13% of the total city tax rate. And finally, a longer-term overview of some of the expected requirements in future years. The 2024 program is currently budgeted at $36.1 million, which includes infrastructure renewal, the continuation of the events centre, and the twinning of a force main. Beyond that, programs of $22.7 million, $26.5 million, And $19.5 million are currently estimated for the following 3 years. That concludes the presentation of the 2023 financial plan. Thank you, members of council. If there are any questions, I can take them now.

lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Every year coming up with a budget is obviously a balancing act because there are many needs within the city. Of course, we also need to be mindful of, of our residents' ability to pay. I think that what we've come up with here is a good budget. For this year, the total

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)
lines.text: Budget is about $34— just over $34 million. There's a lot that we are getting for the money that we're spending. We have a lot of infrastructure renewal happening, and this was mentioned during the presentation. So, for example, underground road— underground infrastructure being repaired, road reconstruction. On Barkman Avenue, for example. The upcoming significant improvements to the Loewen and Highway 12 intersection would come to mind as well. And there's a lot of other things too. In terms of recreation, we know that the event centre is the biggest capital project the city's ever done in our history. It's not even close. The second largest project we've ever done is our secondary water treatment plant, and that was only $11 million. Thank you. And I would say that the reason that we're able to do the event centre at all is because of the fact that this council and past councils for many years have been fiscally responsible and have made sure to spend wisely and to keep debt low. And in particular, our 5-year debt policy. We're continuing with that policy even now, that policy that's been in place for 25, 30 years, and it has paid off in a big way over the years because it means that we are not hamstringing future councils with the, uh, with projects. Rather, we're ensuring that everything is paid off within 5 years, and so that way we're always able to do new things. And that's what we're doing. Other things that we're doing in the budget: we are continuing to have 18 RCMP officers, and of course that's a significant expense, but it's important that we ensure that the city is, uh, is safe. We also are investing in our fire departments, both in terms of the number of firefighters, which The number is at about 49 right now. And of course, continuing to ensure that our firefighters, as was noted earlier, are getting the, the newest and some of the best equipment to ensure that they're able to continue to serve the city well. The municipal mill rate is declining slightly by about 2.8%. Of course, it is a reassessment year, and so that complicates, complicates matters. But in the end, I believe this is a fiscally responsible budget. that at the same time is also aggressive in ensuring that we are meeting the needs of Steinbach today and also in the future. And so I'm happy to make the motion to approve.

lines.text: I will do that, Mr. Mayor and members of council. Yes, this traffic count report is something that council has seen annually for many years. And this document that starts on page 32 of your agenda package represents that annual review. As you did state, it is quite lengthy. There is significant information in it. Thank you. I just wanted to highlight a few sections and— for council's attention. On page 47, that page refers to the weekday PM peak hour traffic volumes. Again, there's consultants that the city hires to review traffic counts, pick representative segments of days and Representative days, typically in October of each year, to do traffic counts to estimate what the typical daily volumes are. And with respect to general traffic volume trends along PTH 12 North and Brandt Street corridor, generally they found that overall traffic volumes along this stretch have increased slightly compared to the pre-pandemic 2019 counts. Thank you. And overall total traffic volumes have increased significantly as compared to 2021 counts. Comparatively, on the PTH 52 West and Main Street corridor, generally overall total traffic volumes along that area have decreased by approximately 3% as compared to the pre-pandemic 2019 counts, with all but one of the intersections counted since 2019 featuring Yes. Featuring lower traffic volumes. So experience in that section of the city was slightly different. Moving on to page 48, you'll see a table, Table 2.1, that looks at significant signalized and unsignalized intersections and the respective counts. I just want to highlight the intersection with the highest activity, which doesn't come as Yeah. A big surprise is Park Road West with the intersection of PTH 12 at a total estimate of 3,620 vehicles per hour. Comparatively, for the currently unsignalized intersections along either PTH 12 or PTH 52, the street, the intersecting street with the highest counts turned out to be Giesbrecht Street with the highest count for that intersection being 1,800 Okay. Moving forward, page 55 in Section 2.2 gives another look at the overall traffic counts, and this particular table represents information that was gathered from weekday AM peak hour traffic volumes. Typically, traffic counts taken during the AM peak hours Yes. And the afternoon hours tend to be generally lower as activity is not found to be quite as robust as the afternoon hours. Moving further through the report, I'll skip ahead to Section 5 and particularly page 67. These consultants reviewed with respect to traffic signal warrant analysis, and these are particularly related to unsignalized intersections with special analysis determining whether or not these existing unsignalized intersections are good candidates for signalization. They do have a historical table on Table 5.1 on page 67. Beginning in 2021, the analysis at the Giesbrecht Street and 50— PTH 52 West intersection indicated that there was sufficient traffic to warrant signalization. And based on the 2022 analysis found a little bit lower down on the page, Table 5.2, that determination was verified again with a traffic warrant analysis. That was confirmed to be required. Beginning on section— in Section 7 on page 72 and then concluding on page 73 is a summation of traffic counts and trends, general observations related to traffic operations, and then finally a section referring to recommendations. I'll highlight the recommendations. Generally, signals are warranted at the intersection of PTH 52 West and Giesbrecht Street, which was indicated in one of the previous tables. And just background for council's information, this was a particular request that city council dealt with in the fall of 2021, at which time a decision was made to make that formal request of Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure, and that department is currently reviewing that request. The latest update that administration has received from that office is that budget funding was not available to see that project be completed in 2023. However, it has been scheduled for 2024. The second recommendation for signalized intersections, as noted, refers to the consultant's analysis on PTH 12 North. And particularly what was found is that signal timing changes based on what is currently there could provide some improvements to the critical movements along that stretch. And again, just as background, in January of this year, that was an item that was identified by City Council. And administration has subsequently contacted Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure to do a further— and request a further review of PTH 12 signalization coordination. My understanding is that office is still undertaking that review and has not yet provided a response to the city. But in all, this— The traffic count report is generally consistent with others that have been presented to the city and to city council before. I'd be happy to answer any other questions council may have.
